rows.text: I agree. Appeasement means giving in to someone to avoid war. Chamberlain met Hitler at Munich in 1938 and gave him the Sudetenland. Hitler also took Austria and sent troops into the Rhineland. Hitler wanted Lebensraum and wrote Mein Kampf. He invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. So there were many reasons why war broke out.

I agree to a large extent. Appeasement was an important reason. Britain and France kept giving in to Hitler to avoid war. In March 1936 he sent troops into the Rhineland, which the Treaty of Versailles had forbidden, and they did nothing. In March 1938 he united Austria with Germany. In September 1938, at the Munich Conference, the British Prime Minister Chamberlain and the French Prime Minister Daladier agreed to give him the Sudetenland, without Czechoslovakia taking part in the talks. In March 1939 Germany took over the rest of the Czech lands. Each success gave Germany more land, soldiers and factories, and convinced Hitler that Britain and France would never fight. This shows appeasement led to war because it encouraged him to gamble on invading Poland. Hitler's aims were also a reason.

Appeasement was an important reason. Britain and France kept giving in to Hitler to avoid war. In March 1936 he sent troops into the Rhineland, which the Treaty of Versailles had forbidden, and they did nothing. In March 1938 he united Austria with Germany. In September 1938, at the Munich Conference, the British Prime Minister Chamberlain and the French Prime Minister Daladier agreed to give him the Sudetenland, without Czechoslovakia taking part in the talks. In March 1939 Germany took over the rest of the Czech lands. Each success gave Germany more land, soldiers and factories, and convinced Hitler that Britain and France would never fight. This shows appeasement led to war because it encouraged him to gamble on invading Poland.

However, Hitler's own aims also led to war. In his book Mein Kampf he had said that he would tear up the Treaty of Versailles, unite all German-speaking people and win living space, or Lebensraum, in the east. He took Germany out of the League of Nations in 1933 and brought back conscription in 1935 to build a large army. In 1939 he demanded the city of Danzig and the Polish Corridor. Britain, with the support of France, promised in March 1939 to defend Poland, yet he still invaded on 1 September 1939. This shows Hitler's aims led to war because living space in the east could only be taken by force.

So both appeasement and Hitler's aims were reasons why war broke out in Europe in 1939.

I agree only to a small extent that appeasement was the main reason. Appeasement was a response to Hitler's demands; it did not create them. If Hitler had wanted only to undo the Treaty of Versailles, giving in might have kept the peace. But his aim of living space in the east went far beyond that, and when Britain, with the support of France, ended appeasement by promising to defend Poland in March 1939, he invaded anyway. Appeasement made Hitler stronger and bolder, but his aims were what made war certain. So Hitler's aims were the main reason.

I agree. The Nazi-Soviet Pact was signed in August 1939 by Germany and the USSR. They agreed not to attack each other. Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939 and Britain and France declared war. Hitler also wanted Danzig and the Polish Corridor. He wanted living space in the east. So there were many reasons why war broke out.

I agree to a large extent. The Nazi-Soviet Pact was an important reason. It was signed on 23 August 1939 by the foreign ministers Ribbentrop and Molotov. Germany and the USSR promised not to attack each other, and in a secret part of the Pact they agreed to divide Poland between them. Hitler's great fear was a war on two fronts, against Britain and France in the west and the USSR in the east, as Germany had faced in the First World War. The Pact removed that fear. Just nine days later, on 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland, and Soviet troops entered from the east on 17 September. This shows the Pact led to war because it left Hitler free to attack Poland. Hitler's demands on Poland were also a reason.

The Nazi-Soviet Pact was an important reason. It was signed on 23 August 1939 by the foreign ministers Ribbentrop and Molotov. Germany and the USSR promised not to attack each other, and in a secret part of the Pact they agreed to divide Poland between them. Hitler's great fear was a war on two fronts, against Britain and France in the west and the USSR in the east, as Germany had faced in the First World War. The Pact removed that fear. Just nine days later, on 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland, and Soviet troops entered from the east on 17 September. This shows the Pact led to war because it left Hitler free to attack Poland.

However, Hitler's own aims and his demands on Poland also led to war. In his book Mein Kampf he had written that Germany must win living space, or Lebensraum, in the east. The Treaty of Versailles had given Poland a strip of land to the sea, the Polish Corridor, which cut East Prussia off from the rest of Germany, and had made Danzig a free city. From late 1938 Hitler demanded that Danzig be returned to Germany, with a road and a railway across the Corridor. Poland refused. Britain, with the support of France, promised in March 1939 to defend Poland, but Hitler did not change course. In April 1939 he ordered his generals to prepare plans for an attack on Poland, months before the Pact was signed. This shows Hitler's aims led to war because he had already decided to settle with Poland by force.

So both the Nazi-Soviet Pact and Hitler's aims and demands on Poland were reasons why war broke out in Europe in September 1939.

I agree only to some extent that the Nazi-Soviet Pact was the main reason war broke out in September 1939. The two factors answer different questions. Hitler's aims explain why there was an attack at all: he had demanded Danzig and the Corridor, and he had ordered plans for an attack in April 1939, four months before the Pact. I agree. After the war the Soviet Union controlled Eastern Europe and there were communist governments in countries like Poland and Hungary. Churchill made a speech about an iron curtain in 1946. The USA had the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan in 1947. The USA was capitalist and the Soviet Union was communist. So there were many reasons for the Cold War.

I agree to a large extent. Soviet actions in Eastern Europe were an important reason. At the Yalta Conference in February 1945 Stalin agreed that the countries freed from Germany would hold free elections. Instead, the Soviet army stayed on in Eastern Europe after 1945, and communist governments loyal to Moscow were set up in Poland, Romania and Bulgaria. The promise of free elections made at Yalta was broken. The West reacted. In March 1946 Churchill warned, in a speech at Fulton in the USA, that an iron curtain had come down across Europe. This shows that Soviet actions made the USA and Britain believe Stalin was breaking his promises and spreading communism, so they began to treat the Soviet Union as an enemy. The Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan were another reason.

Soviet actions in Eastern Europe were an important reason. At the Yalta Conference in February 1945 Stalin agreed that the countries freed from Germany would hold free elections. Instead, the Soviet army stayed on in Eastern Europe after 1945, and communist governments loyal to Moscow were set up in Poland, Romania and Bulgaria. The promise of free elections made at Yalta was broken. The West reacted. In March 1946 Churchill warned, in a speech at Fulton in the USA, that an iron curtain had come down across Europe. This shows that Soviet actions made the USA and Britain believe Stalin was breaking his promises and spreading communism, so they began to treat the Soviet Union as an enemy.

However, American actions also caused the Cold War. In March 1947 President Truman announced the Truman Doctrine: the USA would help any country resisting communism. He asked for 400 million dollars to help Greece and Turkey. In June 1947 the USA announced the Marshall Plan, which gave about 13 billion dollars to help European countries rebuild. Stalin saw this as the USA using its money to win control of Europe and to turn countries against the Soviet Union. He forbade the Eastern European countries to accept the aid, and he tightened his hold in reply. In September 1947 he set up Cominform to keep the communist parties of Europe under Soviet direction. In February 1948 the communists took power in Czechoslovakia. In 1949 he set up Comecon to tie the Eastern European economies to the Soviet Union. This shows that American policy made the Soviet Union feel threatened, so Europe split into two hostile sides.

So both Soviet actions in Eastern Europe and American actions were reasons for the outbreak of the Cold War in Europe.

I agree. The USA was capitalist and the Soviet Union was communist. In a capitalist country people can own businesses and in a communist country the state owns them. The two countries fought together against Germany in the war. There were conferences at Yalta and Potsdam in 1945 and the leaders did not agree on everything. So they became rivals.

I agree to a large extent. Differences in ideology were an important reason. The USA was a capitalist democracy, with free elections and businesses owned by private people. The Soviet Union was a communist state, with one party in power and factories and farms owned by the state. Each side believed its system was the right one for the world and feared that the other would spread. This distrust was old. After the Russian Revolution of 1917, the USA, Britain and other countries had sent troops to help the enemies of the communists in the Russian Civil War. The two powers worked together from 1941 only because they shared an enemy. When Germany surrendered in May 1945 the main reason to work together was gone. This shows that ideology made each side see the other as a danger, so they turned into rivals once the war ended. The leaders also quarrelled at the Potsdam Conference, which was another reason.

This shows that ideology made each side see the other as a danger, so they turned into rivals once the war ended.

However, disagreements during and at the end of the war also turned them into rivals. Stalin had asked his allies to open a second front in Western Europe from 1941, but the landings in France came only in June 1944. The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people in the war, and Stalin suspected that his allies had wanted Germany and the Soviet Union to wear each other out. At the Potsdam Conference in July 1945 the new President, Truman, took a harder line than Roosevelt had. He told Stalin that the USA had a powerful new weapon but did not share the secret of the atomic bomb. The leaders also argued over reparations from Germany and over the government of Poland. This shows that these events built up mistrust between the leaders, so cooperation broke down.

So both differences in ideology and the disagreements during and at the end of the war were reasons why the USA and the Soviet Union became rivals.
